startup.name: Vocality Health
startup.one_liner: Voice AI for medical language translation
startup.description: Voice AI app that lets clinicians speak any language with patients, replacing human medical interpreters and call center interpreter lines. Buyers are hospitals and clinics that already pay billions for in person and remote interpreters. The pitch stresses accuracy and compliance across voice and video. Two person team in San Francisco, Winter 2025 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate about 1 percent for a random applicant (0.6 to 2 percent range, yc_acceptance.md). Adjusted up about 3 times for a clear large paid incumbent market, a specific buyer and a technical voice AI angle. Held back because two founders, no stated traction and hospital sales cycles are slow, and the factor table gives no lift for a pitch alone.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC partners may doubt that a two person team can win hospital procurement, HIPAA review and clinical accuracy standards against LanguageLine and other incumbents. General translation models keep improving, so they may also ask what stays defensible if hospitals can use a foundation model directly.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Window is 22.4 months from 2025-01-06 to 2026-11-17, long enough to cover most of the time to seed distribution (2022 and later p75 is 14.2 months). Starting from the 66 percent ever anchor and the healthcare cohort 50 percent, I hold at 0.48, below the anchor because healthcare has a lower seed rate and a two person team has no stated traction.

bands.rationale: YC deal only, about $500K, and nothing institutional in the window; 13 of 90 confirmed companies in the winners test stopped here.
Small post YC round under $3M from angels or healthtech pre-seed funds while a first hospital pilot is proven.
Institutional seed of $3M to $7M after a pilot or design partner; 2022 and later seed median $3.5M with the YC deal mixed in, so institutional rounds sit higher.
Upside band if a large health system signs and AI voice interest drives a competitive round.

ladder.why_it_fails: The likely miss is that hospitals move slowly: security review, interpreter vendor contracts and clinical validation can take 6 to 12 months, so a two person team may reach month 22 with pilots but no revenue to show a seed investor. Speak and Unbabel show language AI can raise, but Dubjoy shows small translation startups can stall.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Window of 22.4 months is shorter than the 2022 and later median of 28 months to Series A, so the in window chance is about 0.14 against a 35 percent ever anchor, a window effect larger than 2 times. Healthcare cohort conditional is only 9 percent.

bands.rationale: Thin Series A led by a seed fund or a small multi-stage fund, near the 2022 and later median of about $7M with limited revenue proof.
Standard Series A of $8M to $14M after clear revenue growth; the 2018 to 2021 median was $10M and 2022 and later is similar, with era inflation discounted.
Upside band for a breakout in 2025 to 2026 AI categories where rounds are larger than the historical median; a pivot-then-raise path also lands here.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A inside 22 months needs hospital contracts in the millions of dollars. Healthcare AI cohorts of 2022 to 2025 show only one in ten seed companies reaching Series A, because pilots rarely convert to enterprise revenue quickly and general model vendors compress the price of translation.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --calibration-only: series_b cond 44% (n=126), ever not windowed.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Near the anchor times 0.8; ever reached step beyond the window.

bands.rationale: Flat or modest Series B after slower growth than the Series A plan assumed.
Typical Series B of $20M to $40M on proven repeatable growth.
Upside band for a category leader whose growth outpaces peers and attracts a competitive multi-stage process.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B would need a national footprint of hospitals and an AI interpreter that replaces a large share of human minutes at a profit. Incumbents with existing contracts can bundle AI interpreting, so growth could flatten before the scale investors expect, as Unbabel found when generative AI compressed its revenue.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Slightly under the anchor, healthcare services AI rarely scales past B in the data.

bands.rationale: Smaller Series C or extension, close to a flat round.
Standard growth round for a company with real scale.
Upside band for a market leader with strong growth and margins that can command a premium at late stage.

ladder.why_it_fails: A growth round needs a path to hundreds of millions in revenue, but language access is a cost center for hospitals and per minute prices fall as models improve. Unbabel reached Series C and then shrank, which is the pattern for a language AI business without a durable moat.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely result is a stall or a small acquisition: hospitals buy language access on price per minute, foundation model vendors cut costs, and compliance expectations favour large incumbents. Unbabel and Dubjoy show language AI companies end small or shut down when the model layer commoditizes.

analogs.outcome_summary: Raised through Series C and was acquired after revenue dropped when machine translation became cheap.
Inactive with no funding round found; shows the commodity risk.
Raised a Series B in 2022 on strong product pull, a better case for voice AI.
Raised a $2M seed in June 2024 right after YC.

killers.evidence: Hospitals require security, privacy and clinical review before deploying new tools and most voice tools go through pilots.
killers.mitigation: Land one health system champion and sell narrow use cases first, such as intake.

killers.evidence: General translation and speech models improve quickly, which lowers the price of the core capability and brings in large model vendors.
killers.mitigation: Own compliance, clinical vocabulary and workflow integration.

killers.risk: Accuracy and liability in clinical settings
killers.evidence: A mistranslation can harm a patient, and buyers ask for evidence that AI matches certified human interpreters.
killers.mitigation: Publish validation studies and keep human escalation.

technical_complexity.rationale: Real time speech to speech with clinical accuracy, low latency, rare languages and diarization is hard, and errors have patient safety cost. A two person team can ship a demo with off the shelf models but proving compliance and accuracy takes months.

takeover_risk.rationale: Incumbent interpreter companies already have hospital contracts and can add AI, and large model vendors can match the base translation. A startup advantage would have to be clinical accuracy and workflow fit.

evidence.claim: One source puts US spending on formal medical interpretation at about 3.8 billion dollars a year, a vendor claim
A Princeton note says 97 percent of hospitals see limited English patients and 46 percent lack translation services

actions: Sign two health systems at per minute pricing
roadmap.proof: Annual contract value per site and pilots converting to paid

pros.evidence: Hospitals must provide language access and already spend on interpreters.

brand.name: Vocality Health
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Vocality Health" --era 2022+: 14 characters, 2 words, name plus descriptor
weaknesses: Generic compared with invented brand names
brand.rationale: A name plus descriptor shows the category at once, which helps trust in a regulated market, but it is less ownable than a short invented name. It neither helps nor hurts the funding odds much.

narrative.headline: A real, paid problem with slow hospital buyers; seed in 22 months is a bit under even and Series A is unlikely.
narrative.general_summary: Vocality sells voice AI interpretation to hospitals that already pay for human interpreters. The need is large and legal, the technical bar is high and incumbents can add AI. The 22.4 month window is long enough for a seed round above $1M to land if a pilot converts, but a Series A inside it is unlikely. The odds do not rank this company against others in the batch because the anchor is the cohort rate. The main risks are hospital procurement time, commoditization and accuracy liability.
